intro: Isolde sees the dead Tristan as if he were alive, then hears a sound that the other characters cannot hear. Larsen-Todsen’s 1928 recording preserves the vocal scene, not the familiar orchestra-only concert arrangement; it is a different performance from this set’s Prelude.
question: How does a sequence of renewed surges become a final, quiet arrival?

cues.title: A voice above trembling strings
cues.text: Isolde begins “Mild und leise” — softly and gently — over a restrained orchestral texture. Low strings tremble beneath the vocal line; the score introduces the bass clarinet before gradually admitting brighter colours.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf vocal-and-orchestral excerpt score, p. 14: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070. Opening identification; detailed cue timing is passage-level.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow a whole breath
cues.text: Listen for the direction of each long vocal phrase, not just its highest note. The orchestra has its own rising lines, so a breath in the singing need not halt the musical ascent.
cues.evidence: General listening prompt based on the separate vocal and orchestral lines in score pp. 14–17: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A named historical cast
cues.text: The Preiser sleeve identifies the Bayreuth Festival Orchestra and Karl Elmendorff for this Liebestod. It gives Columbia L 2206 as the original record; conductors listed for other tracks on the album do not belong to this performance.
cues.evidence: https://archive.org/download/nanny-larsen-todsen-preiser-lv-174-side-a/Larsen-Todsen%20Preiser%20%282%29.JPG; “Mild und leise” entry names the orchestra, conductor, year and original catalogue.

cues.title: A swell gives way
cues.text: The sound pulls back after the first broad rise. Compare that release with the Prelude’s pauses: here the voice remains part of a continuous dramatic scene rather than a series of isolated orchestral questions.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −9.6 dB at 1:50 falls to −21.3 dB at 1:55; further renewed activity follows around 2:20–2:30.

cues.title: Expansion is not yet arrival
cues.text: Another surge reaches a local crest and retreats. Wagner repeatedly enlarges the phrase instead of treating its high point as a final cadence; the largest wave is still ahead.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −9.5 dB at 2:25, falling to −23.7 dB by 2:45. Formal interpretation is passage-level, not a chord identification.

cues.title: A Bayreuth Isolde
cues.text: Larsen-Todsen’s Bayreuth Isolde in 1928 belongs to the period of this recording. The reissue sleeve presents the recorded Tristan as an important surviving document of her leading Wagner roles.
cues.evidence: https://archive.org/download/nanny-larsen-todsen-preiser-lv-174-side-a/Larsen-Todsen%20Preiser%20%282%29.JPG; Dr Anton Odelga’s biographical note discusses the 1928 Bayreuth Isolde and Elmendorff recording.

cues.title: Hear the next wave gather
cues.text: Listen across the quieter passage into the next increase in force. The transition matters as much as the peak: sustained lines and repeated rising shapes make the new wave feel like a continuation, not a fresh beginning.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −24 dB at 3:45 and −23 dB at 3:50 rise to −8 dB at 4:00. Score pp. 22–24 shows the accumulating vocal and orchestral lines.

cues.title: Voice and orchestra together
cues.text: At the fuller points, ask which line carries your attention: the soprano’s words or the orchestra’s continuing melody. Wagner’s score gives both directional work; accompaniment is not merely a quiet support beneath a solo.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 24–27: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070. General orchestral relationship; no individual doubling is claimed at 4:26.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The highest wave
cues.text: The strongest recorded crest comes in this late span. Compare it with the earlier rises: the music has trained the ear to expect renewal, yet the ending will ultimately be quieter, not louder.
cues.evidence: Analysis: strongest five-second window at 5:20, −6.4 dB; earlier substantial crest at 4:10, −7.8 dB.

cues.title: A death seen differently
cues.text: The stage situation is not a reunion in ordinary life: Tristan is dead. Isolde’s words turn sight into imagined sound and finally dissolution; the orchestra carries the scene beyond what the other characters can perceive.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde synopsis of Act III; the vocal text appears in the excerpt score, pp. 14–30.

cues.title: A different kind of resolution
cues.text: The scene’s written destination is B major. Unlike the Prelude’s opening, the conclusion permits a stable tonic to remain; the long delay makes the restrained ending carry the weight that another climax might otherwise supply.
cues.evidence: Score p. 30: B-major final cadence. This cue concerns the concluding passage, not a chord asserted at 6:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wait beyond the final word
cues.text: Let the orchestral ending complete the scene after the text reaches its last thought. The concluding resonance and the space after it belong to the arrival, rather than serving as disposable silence.
cues.evidence: Score p. 30 continues after the final sung “Lust”. Analysis falls to −44.8 dB at 7:20 and −71.3 at 7:25. Vocal release is not separately time-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A local retreat releases another ascent
transitions.how: The opening grows through rising vocal phrases and increasingly active string writing. A local reduction of force allows another expansion: recurring melodic shapes connect the spans while fuller orchestration changes their scale. This is renewed motion, not the final B-major cadence.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 14–20; analysis boundary 2:20 and local crest 2:25. Approximate subdivision of a continuous scene.

transitions.title: Quieter phrases feed a larger wave
transitions.how: After a quieter passage, rising figures and fuller orchestral support carry the voice towards a larger crest. The accompaniment continues across phrase boundaries, preventing each vocal breath from sounding like the end of the musical sentence.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 22–24; analysis level rises sharply between 3:50 and 4:00.

transitions.title: Repeated rises reach their greatest weight
transitions.how: The score’s late intensification expands the same upward-directed material with brilliant string and wind figuration. The increase in orchestral weight supports the culminating vocal span; the accumulated wave, rather than a new contrasting theme, produces the climax.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 26–28; strongest measured window 5:20. Page-to-recording placement is approximate.

transitions.title: The crest gives way to a quiet arrival
transitions.how: The orchestra relinquishes the preceding force and extends the closing line towards B major. The voice eventually falls silent, leaving the orchestra to complete the cadence. A sustained quiet tonic, not a final burst of volume, supplies the decisive difference from the Prelude’s opening.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 29–30; level falls markedly by 5:50–5:55. The final cadence is later within this span, not precisely at its start.

source.title: Wagner: Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, with vocal part — Breitkopf & Härtel
source.locator: Printed pp. 14–30; broad score-proportion landmarks, not bar-synchronised entrances.

timeline.note: Opening span, p. 14: low tremolando strings support Isolde; bass clarinet and trombones enter softly.
Approximate first expansion, pp. 15–17: brighter woodwind and harp join the string-and-voice texture.
Approximate middle span: woodwind responses and active inner strings accompany the continuing vocal line.
Broad accumulating span, pp. 24–27: harp, woodwind and strings remain active as brass reinforces the rises.
Late climactic region, pp. 27–28; the timestamp marks the strongest audio crest, not each instrumental entrance.

Final orchestral cadence, p. 30. The voice has finished; quiet wind and string lines settle into the final chords. Cor anglais and timpani contribute within this closing region, not continuously throughout it.

facts: Composition with Theodor Weinlig in Leipzig; practical theatre work in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga
Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, Dresden, 1843–49; founder of the Bayreuth Festival, first held in 1876
Wrote his own librettos, alongside extensive and often polemical prose
Thirteen completed operas; the four-part Ring; songs, orchestral works and piano music
composer.background:
Wagner grew up among actors, singers and theatrical households in Leipzig and Dresden. His father died in 1813; his mother subsequently married the actor and painter Ludwig Geyer. Literature preceded serious musical training: as a schoolboy Wagner attempted a tragedy before he had mastered composition. Beethoven’s symphonies and Weber’s operas supplied different models, one for the weight of an orchestral argument, the other for a German theatre of supernatural events and sharply characterised instruments. Lessons with Theodor Weinlig in 1831 gave him a grounding in counterpoint. The later claim to have rebuilt opera came from someone who first learned its routines as a working theatre musician.

He held posts in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga, married the actress Minna Planer in 1836, and repeatedly found himself in debt. His early operas tried incompatible languages: Die Feen follows German Romantic opera, while Das Liebesverbot, after Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, adopts a more Italianate manner. In 1839 the Wagners fled Riga and travelled by sea to London, then to Paris. There he copied, arranged and wrote journalism while trying to enter the operatic establishment. Meyerbeer, whom Wagner would later attack, helped him obtain a hearing for Rienzi. Wagner knew the grand-opera machinery of public ceremony, political catastrophe and large chorus from practical experience.
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made the orchestra remember what the characters conceal, and built a theatre for the result.
